en: The Philippine eagle, the national bird, uses its massive talons and sharp vision to hunt flying lemurs and other small animals in the rainforest.
The parasitic plant Rafflesia schadenbergiana, found in Mount Kitanglad, produces the world's largest individual flower but lacks leaves, stems, and roots.
Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea protects over six hundred species of fish and three hundred species of corals.
Filipino pediatrician Dr. Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator to help keep premature babies warm in rural areas without electricity.
The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes that are larger than its brain, allowing it to see clearly and hunt insects at night.
The bakawan mangrove tree drops fully germinated seedlings directly into the coastal mud so they can quickly take root in shallow water.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito transmits the dengue virus to humans by biting them during the day, especially in the early morning and late afternoon.
The Pawikan, or sea turtle, returns to the exact Philippine beach where it hatched to lay its own eggs in the sand.
The Philippine pitcher plant, Nepenthes alata, uses modified leaves shaped like deep cups to trap and digest insects for extra nutrients.
The butanding, or whale shark, is the largest fish in the world and visits Donsol to filter-feed on tiny plankton.
The lagundi plant, officially endorsed by the Philippine Department of Health, contains compounds that effectively relieve coughs and asthma symptoms.
The tamaraw, a critically endangered buffalo endemic to Mindoro, has V-shaped horns and shorter legs to help it navigate dense mountain forests.
